utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzafic, you say that those people were disarmed and that the same day, two buses arrived in the village, and --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The paramilitary formations. What kind of paramilitaries were they?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And which people were disarmed on that day? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the day when they were taken into custody and taken to the police station, those people, that day.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been brought in the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when the paramilitary formations arrived, nobody was taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which paramilitary formations were they?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were soldiers belonging to the territorial Serbian defence, and it was related, in fact, to my neighbours. They were the ones who took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these were people you knew, as far as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know them all?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 90 per cent of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they were all from the Bratunac municipality, were they? That's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 90 per cent of them were people living around my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 4, paragraph 1 of your statement that while you were waiting in Bratunac, a certain Fadil Habibovic was called. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was he? Why was he called? Why was his name called out by the people who were there? I assume you knew him too because you all knew each other there. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who took him away, took him off you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. You say that they were all your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The person who took Fadil Habibovic away, I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Habibovic had been taken to the house in Krasno Polje; that is right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say he was killed there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be of assistance? It's paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that he was taken to his home in Krasno Polje and killed there.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who I heard it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for him to have been taken back?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to what some people said, Fadil Habibovic was a well-to-do man. He was well off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that could have been the reason, is that it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say so, yes, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see what actually happened to him?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just -- I just saw him being taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And another man, Omer Muminovic was also called out, shall is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these two men was anybody else's name called out?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that nothing happened to this man Muminovic.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he came back?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Muminovic, whose name was called out, returned. Habibovic did not return, and you heard that somebody killed him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he was killed by Novo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say? Who killed him?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is this Novo man?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My neighbour and a former taxi driver in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say that on that occasion, a military rucksack was found with Jasmin Muminovic and that he was taken to the MUP for interrogation. Was he relation, this man Jasmin Muminovic, with this man Omer Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Omer was taken over there and released. And what happened to Jasmin?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jasmin was taken to the Vlasenica police station. He was interrogated and then released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was taken in too because of the military equipment that was found on him and then released.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of equipment he had. He just had a military rucksack because he had come back several days before that from doing his Yugoslav People's Army military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you say that 32 prisoners, males, men who were military-able men, as you say, they were taken to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to the MUP, to the premises of the MUP, and it was a sort of prison, a MUP prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But was it within the frameworks of the MUP building itself?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was next door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A regular prison?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether it was a prison or not, I don't know. But I felt it to be a prison. I was never in Vlasenica myself. I was never at the police station there or the prison there so I can't say, but that's what it felt like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say the cell you were put up in was about 3 by 5 metres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately between 3 and 5 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And 32 of you went inside plus another five soldiers who came to beat you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't soldiers, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were these civilians then?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were brought in later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were those civilians from your parts too?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, please, how was it possible that in this small room, 3 by 5 metres, you had 32 prisoners and five civilians? How could all this be going on there? How could they be beaten in such a small room?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all civilians in the room, so it wasn't 32 men plus five civilians. They were all civilians. There were 37 of us in all. And yes, it was possible. Everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the answer that everything's possible, yes. Tell me this now, please, to move on to the actual event when you say a certain Macedonian boarded the bus in which you were put up and said -- and told you to step down by the back door in groups of four and five. I think you say that on page 6, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was right next to the entrance to Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you were in town when you refer to this?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say at the entrance to Kasaba. So you were far from -- you weren't far from town. When you say Kasaba, it refers to the old part of down; right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a big town. It's a very small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A small town then. So you were at this entrance to this small town; right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that the first group stepped down from the bus and that the soldiers killed them there on the spot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right at the entrance to this small town, is that it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance to the small town, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And from what distance did they shoot?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I didn't have time to count the metres and steps or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you have some idea, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have some idea. The bus was parked on the asphalt road. There was one group of people standing by the back door to the bus. The others were in front of the bus. There was an APC in front of the bus, and it took part in the shooting. And as the people got off, they would pass across the fields and that's when they shot, did the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you shot at straight after you got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was getting off the bus, I heard an order being called out that we should flee across the fields, escape across the fields, run across the fields. So I managed to get a little away from the asphalt road, because the people who were first and stepped down from the bus first were right up by the asphalt, and then you get to the field and that's where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's something that doesn't seem to be quite clear to me there, because you say that as they got off the bus, somebody shot at them.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not somebody shot. We know who shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you described who those people were a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those people who expelled me from the village weren't the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't link all this up now. Does that mean that it wasn't the people who expelled you and brought you there who shot you? Who did shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who expelled me from the village were not there when this execution took place. The people had come in -- actually, other people had come into Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who were these other people who came into Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I learnt later on they were members of the Vukovar diversionary or sabotage platoon. And I mentioned that they were wearing uniforms the Arkan Tiger type and the White Eagles. People in uniforms, the olive-green uniforms. And I knew one of them personally. He was a neighbour of mine and his name was Pero Mitrovic, and he was an active participant in the event and he was wearing the olive-green uniform. And as I had done my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, I could recognise that he had a sniper on him too, and I noticed that another man was wearing shorts. There were people who wore masks. This other man had a cape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was one in a cape. Others were wearing shorts?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were all sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were wounded in different -- in four different parts of your body from an automatic weapon and a heavy machine-gun. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wounded in four parts of my body on the right-hand side. So the right-hand side of my body received four gunshot wounds, and one of them was caused by the heavy machine-gun that was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you exactly wounded?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My stomach, my hip, leg, two bullets to my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any medical documents to prove that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have visible scars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know which of the weapons hit you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just do. I know that this APC and the bullet came from there, and the wound was inflicted from a higher altitude, from -- the shot came from up above, and it was actually the machine-gun fire that hit me from the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on this situation here, because in the statement you gave on the 15th of June, 1993, in the security centre of Tuzla, you describe this event in a different way.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that statement, on page 5, you claim that you heard shooting coming from the APC and that you saw a group being taken out of the bus and ordered to move towards the nearby field.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that, because it didn't happen that way. It happened the way I described a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have your statement here from that centre in Tuzla. It's not very legible, the copy, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does the Chamber want a copy if it doesn't already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't a copy. We ought to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the witness ought to have -- I don't know if we've got a B/C/S version available for him. We have -- it's also on page 5, both the English and the B/C/S, and I will hand in the -- hand to the usher the B/C/S version for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say towards the end of that page: "I saw that a group had also been taken out of the bus and they were ordered to move to the field."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... eight lines down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the group that I got out with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you identify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's page 5 in the English, but it's about eight lines down from the top. "I saw that a group had already been taken off the bus," I think that's the passage he's referring to, "and had been ordered to head toward the field."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: Did they shoot at them from the spot or did they order them to move towards the field? I can't align these two statements, because a moment ago you said it wasn't correct, but that's what it says here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Don't confuse the witness. Have you got -- just a moment. Have you got the passage, Mr. Dzafic, in the statement to the security centre? Have you identified the passage? You see here it says that one -- "I saw one group being taken off and had been ordered to head towards the field. The Serbian soldiers shot at their backs and the people fell to the ground." Then the next sentence reads: "Five or six people at a time were taken off the bus and chased into the field, after which they were gunned down by bursts of fire from automatic rifles and anti-aircraft machine-guns." Now, do you want to make any comment about that, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not taken into the field, that is to say, they were shot after as soon as they got off the bus, which means that they were given a bit of leeway. They could go a bit in front of the soldiers and then they were shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you, because you say that they went about 30 or 40 metres away, and in the statement you say that they were being shot at on the spot, as soon as they got off the bus. So what is true?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that my group of five or six men that was the last to get off the bus managed to move about 30 to 40 metres away from the asphalt road, because that was the last group to get off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But in the statement given to the investigators, you say that you were hit as soon as you got off the bus. And in the statement given to the authorities in Tuzla, you say that you were ordered to run and that you managed to cross 30 or 40 metres. What is true?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not hit on the bus. I was hit when I got off the bus. So it's in this type period. It wasn't minutes, it was a question of seconds. I got off the bus and then the order was to run across the field and that's it. That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as you say, those men who were shooting at you were looking for survivors.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they shot from pistols.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At every group?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they looking for survivors after they shot at every group or after you had been hit?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the last group to get off, so when it was all over, then they set out to look for survivors, to see whether anybody had survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They managed to get to you right at the moment when they started quarreling between themselves. That is what you say on paragraph 13, page 6?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When they reached you, they managed to quarrel somewhere when they were there between you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't right next to me. It was, say, within a radius of 10 to 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they quarreled and they --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then they did what they did. They checked who survived and Mitrovic and Makedonac had quarreled amongst themselves. They said this should not have happened by the main road. And then I just heard a voice that they should get on to the vehicles and leave. And I heard this group of vehicles and then, all of a sudden, there was silence. Then I got up. Then I raised my head, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that after they left you lay on the ground for two more hours?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I needed two hours to get to the place where I stayed. And after me, these other two survivors came. They came two hours after I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last paragraph on page 6. You say: "I lay on the ground for two more hours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness made the correction to that paragraph. He said: "I got up immediately and tried to go in the direction of a nearby Muslim hamlet."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, which statement are you now referring to? You've referred to page 6. Is this the security centre or are you referring to the OTP statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The statement made to the investigators here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is paragraph 50, paragraph 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have it together with the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not lie for another two hours. When they got off, then you got up and left.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, then I set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then, since you were wounded in four different places, you had two wounds in your leg and one in the hip, is that right, and one wound was in the stomach, is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you went to a village?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which village is this?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left without knowing where I was going. I was looking for a village in order to seek shelter. Celikovic is the village concerned. A small village, just a few houses, and that's where I got to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far away is this village from the site where everything happened?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. It took me two hours approximately to get there. Probably if I were healthy and if everything were all right, I would have gotten there in, say, about 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You would walk with all those four wounds?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to walk, because I tried to lie down but I couldn't because of the pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "After a while, two other survivors were brought to the village."

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who brought them?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this statement that you made in Tuzla, you say that they had lighter wounds.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of wounds were they?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rahman Karic had an exit/entry wound here on the left arm, and Sado Muhic was just grazed by a bullet on his arm. Only his skin was grazed. And this wound was caused by a pistol. Because they were telling me when they were getting off, they were not hit but then they were actually wounded when those men were going around to check whether there were any survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They stayed after you at the site where all this had taken place?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those men who had lighter wounds stayed there on the spot and they stayed after you, and you, although you had more serious wounds, managed to leave earlier on?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I couldn't lie there because of the pain. I had to get up immediately. And it was probably fear and everything else because of everything that had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, actually, since you spoke about this here and you gave a list of persons - all of them are men, actually, men from your area - are these men who were killed in fighting while they were a part of Naser Oric's units? Is that the case rather than them being executed? There was no execution.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, I'm asking you whether these men were actually killed in fighting in the units of Naser Oric in that area. They were not executed.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which fighting? Which units?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that area, there were Muslim --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the men on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's suggested, Mr. Dzafic, and you should have the chance to deal with it, it's suggested there was no execution at all, is what the accused is saying. Now, is there any truth, is there any possibility of that being so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The execution did take place, and these men who are on the list were executed during that execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're claiming that these men on the list were not in Naser Oric's units and were not killed in combat? You're saying that they were executed by these other people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard that. That's what he says. We've heard that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about the requirement of surrendering of arms. Tell us, when the man came to require that you surrender arms, did he have lists?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you get to know what was on the lists at some stage?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He held the lists in his hands, and he said, "According to this list you had been issued weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any truth to that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to this suggestion by the accused that you made up this entire story of the execution, how many family members of yours were included in those who died as they came off that bus?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ninety per cent of them were relatives and family. From my very own house were my father and two brothers who were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what the accused is suggesting, your father, yourself, your two brothers, amongst others, were fighting for Naser Oric and that they were killed and you were injured, I suppose, in the course of that fighting. Any truth in that suggestion at all?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true. The truth is that we were captured at home and that they were taken out there and killed as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I ask. I observe that the accused even challenged whether the witness was injured. The witness effectively offered inspection of his injuries, but I'm not proposing to go to that detail. It seems inappropriate in the setting of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's all I ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll give an exhibit number to the -- the next D number for the state security services statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 153, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm just debating whether in fact it might be more convenient to make it a Prosecution Exhibit. The practice has already been to make these Defence statements, but I wonder whether it's not more convenient to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For retrieval purposes it might be simpler to add it right after the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the package, as it were, of statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm tempted to do that. I didn't re-examine on the alleged differences. It seems to me that they may have been rather more seeming than real.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Make it so. Make it so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 474.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff will be calling the next witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. May this witness be released?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, the Court's grateful to you for coming here to give your evidence. It is now concluded, and you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is General Imra Agotic, and he will testify without protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit 475. That's for the exhibit of documents for witness Imra Agotic, Exhibit 475.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to explain to you, we have provided the new exhibits, and you find them in one bundle and then you find the courtesy copy for those already discussed, and you have also a few maps. And you can see it in the proofing summary how they are marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Imra Agotic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before the war, had you been a professional soldier in the JNA and later in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you retire from the Croatian army and with which rank?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I retired on the 2nd of July, 1991, with the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's from the JNA. And when did you retire from the Croatian army and with which rank?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I retired from the Croatian army on the 30th of December, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With which rank?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: With the rank of lieutenant colonel, a four-star general.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Besides being a professional soldier, do you also have a Masters Degree from the Faculty of Political Science of the University of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a Masters Degree in international relations in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I am currently advisor to the president of the Republic of Croatia for national security.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the preparation of your testimony, did you, together with staff from the Prosecution office, provide and list -- did you make a listing of your personal and professional background?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's tab 1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you review this document, and is it correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I did, and what I have in front of me is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before May 1990, were the -- this is enough, sir. It's -- that was -- we can put this exhibit aside. In -- before May 1990, were the weapons of the TO stored, where were they stored, and who had control over them?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite hear the last part of your question, the interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were the weapons of the TO stored before May 1990, and who had control over them?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: You mean the weapons of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The weapons of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia, up until May 1991, were held in warehouses of the TO of the Republic of Croatia. And the commanders, the officers in the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia had the right to use them and control them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness Exhibit 447, tab 3. It's an order from General Adzic of the 14th May 1990 regarding the transfer of the weapons and ammunition of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I am, but in the course of 1990, I did not see it because I wasn't in office to be able see it then. But I did see it later on when I joined the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says here in the little paragraph above the word "Order," there is a reference that it is about safe storage and safekeeping of the weapons. Were the weapons at that time stored unsafe in the TO warehouses?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: In the sense of safety, they were well-protected in the warehouses, and I know this also on the basis of the report of the main inspection, which took place several months before this event, that is when the weapons were taken over, and who went to check some of the warehouses of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is also a reference in this -- in the first paragraph of the order where there is said that, "In the absence of space in the dumps of depots, use the most suitable premises within the area of those dumps and depots," and there's also even a reference to using rooms in the barracks. Is -- were these places indicated here, in particular the rooms, were they more safe than what -- than the TO warehouses?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The gist of this first paragraph and of the whole order was not to place it under safer conditions as far as guarding the weapons was concerned. The aim of it was, in fact, to replace the TO guards and the guards of the Ministry of the Interior who were guarding those warehouses up until then with JNA guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There in paragraph 2 there is also a reference to exceptional cases where TO weapons would remain outside of the JNA depots, and it says here: "They should be stored and safeguarded in the TO depots guarded by JNA units." What effect did that have?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That is quite correct, and this confirms what I've just said, that the aim was to change the guards, for another company, in quotation marks, to control the weapons. And the effect of it was that the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia was disempowered in terms of controlling its own property.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatian government comply with this order?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The order was fully complied with, and all that remained at the disposal of the Croatian government was in a warehouse or in a company in Zagreb called Mega, and it amounted to some 30 rifles, because they refused to hand them over. All the others in Croatia did hand their weapons over to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we don't have or I don't have in my binder the Adzic order. We have the report. I have the report of the colonel, but I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have a separate bundle with a green cover. Those were the exhibits that were already tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd make it plain. I've got it now. Perhaps you'd make it plain.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next document is tab 2. This is in the bundle of new documents, Your Honour. Tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, I would like you briefly to just look at this. This seems to be an example of compliance with the order, and it refers to the municipality of Split and the compliance is, as it says here, achieved, and the date is the 21 of May, 1990. Is that just one example of numerous similar letters?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is correct. This was the way that the implementation of tasks were reported. In this case, it was the handing over of the ammunition of the Territorial Defence to JNA warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many weapons the TO actually transferred in May 1990? Just a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The TO of the Republic of Croatia handed over to JNA control about 180.000 rifles, which means light weaponry with long barrels. It handed over about 60 mortars, a large number of anti-aircraft guns, in fact, all those that it had at its disposal. These were small calibre guns of 20 millimetres and all the ammunition that it had at that time. And this was up to five combat sets, which means several million rounds ranging from small to the largest calibres.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said already that you left the JNA on the 2nd of July, 1991. Was that on your own request, and if so, why did you want to leave?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That is right. I wrote a request on the 2nd of July in the morning, and in the afternoon I was informed that a decision had been taken granting me permission to leave. This was because of the JNA operations in Slovenia. That was the last drop that when I lost patience and decided no longer to remain an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You did then join the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That's right. I offered my services to the government of the Republic of Croatia. I was received by the president, and he said that for five days I should be his military advisor. Five days later, he ordered me to take over the command over the National Guards Corps, that is, to be the Chief of Staff of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you serve in this position?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I remained Chief of Staff and commander of the National Guards Corps until the 21st of September, 1991, when the Main Staff of the Croatian army was formed and General Anton Tus was then appointed head of that General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you joined the ZNG, what was its strength as to manpower, and what about weapons?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The National Guards Corps was formed within the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Croatia, and at that point in time when I joined it, it had four brigades which were about 80 per cent filled to capacity in terms of personnel, which meant between 8.000 and 9.000 men, and about -- it had 30 per cent of the required quantity of long-barrel weapons. And when I say that, I mean rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the state of organisation of these brigades? Were these professional soldiers and the organisation as such?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The National Guards Corps, at first, was formed immediately as a professional army. People joined on a voluntary basis. While I was commander of the guards, people joined as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it a highly organised organisation when you joined or was it -- what was the standard of organisation?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the National Guards Corps was composed at the beginning of men who did not have military knowledge or military training or were not graduates of military schools, it could not be organised in the way it was later on after training had been completed and after some combat experience had been gained. So that one can say that the National Guards Corps in those days was not sufficiently well trained, but it had a great deal of commitment to the defence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Had General Spegelj purchased weapons before you joined the ZNG, and can you say anything about the amount and the kind of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: When I joined, there was a certain amount of weaponry within the National Guards Corps. The popular Kalashnikovs, which are long-barrel weapons, then also the guards had about 8.000 of those weapons. But from conversations I had later on with General Spegelj, I learnt that in the period when he and men around him were procuring weapons, about 20.000 rifles were procured of those rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Had General Spegelj tried to purchase weapons legally through the federal organs, and if so, what was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: After the Territorial Defence had been disarmed, General Spegelj, being the Defence Minister of the Republic of Croatia, requested through a formal letter or request from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence that weapons be procured for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, because it has to be known that the National Guards Corps was not formed until the 28th of May, 1991, which means the request was made for the Ministry Internal Affairs, not for the guards. There were either no responses or that request was not met with in the way that was customary to procure weapons in -- within the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you clarify this, please, General. You said that the ZNG had 30 per cent of the long-barrelled weapons required, but you also said that they had 8.000 Kalashnikovs, and you say that there were about 8.000 to 9.000 men in the ZNG. Now, it may be that you are talking about different times, but could you please just explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since about 20.000 of those Kalashnikovs were obtained in the period prior to the formation of the National Guards Corps, these weapons were used to arm units of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that had existed within the forces of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Republic of Croatia to deal with internal affairs. When the National Guards Corps was formed at the end of May 1991, again under the auspices and within the Ministry of Internal Affairs, one battalion within each of these brigades was armed, and that is why I say that only about 30 per cent of all the personnel had weapons, because there was a large influx of men and the weapons had already been distributed to this battalion of National Guards Corps within each brigade and also some to units of the Ministry of Internal Affairs for whom those weapons had originally been intended. So there may be an apparent discrepancy in the numbers because of this. By way of an example, within the 1st brigade that was stationed in Zagreb or in the environs in Zagreb, when I took over duty, I had only one battalion fully armed. And in fact there was manpower for four battalions because people were voluntarily joining at a fast pace. So that those who did not have weapons, and there was no way to obtain them, had to get round the problem in various ways. For instance, getting hunting weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you've clarified it. Yes. Can we move on, please, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to at approval of the SSNO that you've mentioned, did that apply to both, that means the request for weapons for the TO and requests for weapons of the police? Would the SSNO always have to approve it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That was procedure. The SSNO was the body that would approve or give approval whether a particular unit would be armed, replenished, re-armed, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the SSNO control the companies that produced weapons throughout the former Yugoslavia in this way?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That is right. That was the so-called special purpose industry which was under the command of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you noticed that there was a lack of arms, did you brief President Tudjman about it, and did you make suggestions for the purchase of weapons?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I did. Among the first requests that I made of President Tudjman, who was at the time Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, thereby also of the National Guards Corps, was that in view of the situation that existed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia at the time, there were many barricades, roadblocks, that Croatia already controlled only 30 per cent of its territory [as interpreted], I requested that weapons and ammunition be obtained for the personnel within the National Guards Corps. President Tudjman, in August 1991, responded, "Don't hurry. There won't be any war. We'll come to an agreement. We'll solve the problems and the situation peacefully." Unfortunately, that did not come about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did he believe that he would come to an agreement, and agreement with whom? Did he say something about that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I was not involved in any political issues, and I didn't know at the time who he negotiated with, but I do know that there were many sessions of the SFRY Presidency, some of which he attended, and I know and I heard later that he had frequent telephone contacts, maybe some others as well, with the Serbian leadership, which in our judgement was the partner with which to negotiate the situation in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to clarify one point that I see in the transcript. You said that at that time, the Croatian -- the Croatian authorities controlled only 30 per cent of its territory. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I said that it did not control 30 per cent of its territory. It did control the rest of its territory. So about 30 per cent of its territory was under blockade of the Serb rebels within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After the war had started, did the Croatian forces capture weapons from the JNA, and if so, how was that done?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Partly the Croatian forces seized weapons from the JNA because they captured some barracks by force. Once it became clear that war was raging throughout Croatia and that the JNA had sided with the Serb rebels in Croatia, a second part of the weaponry that Croatia received by the end of 1991 to arm units of the Croatian army were weapons of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia that were returned, a part of those weapons at least, as a result of negotiations with authorised negotiators of the Yugoslav People's Army in Zagreb, which started on the 8th of October, 1991. And they were based on a Hague agreement of the 4th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which period did the Croatian army get back TO weapons? You said it started in October 1991, but in which time period did they actually receive the weapons from the TO?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: In the extent to which the JNA units withdrew from the Republic of Croatia, the arms were handed over to the Croatian army, that is to say the weapons that belonged to the Territorial Defence of Croatia. And the last unit to withdraw from the territory of the Republic of Croatia was from Vis and Lastovo, and this took place sometime in January 1992. However, the largest portion withdrew at the end of 1991. And when I'm speaking about withdrawal, what I am referring to is that part of the territory of the Republic of Croatia which was under the control of Croatia -- the Croatian authorities itself -- themselves, which is the 70 per cent of the territory that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you get back the full amount of weapons that you previously had transferred or less?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I don't have the exact figures, but I do know that certain warehouses where the weapons were stored belonging to the Territorial Defence of Croatia from -- in May 1991 when it was confiscated, that they were blown up by the Yugoslav People's Army. For example, the depot at Rijeka, the depot at Gorski Kotar in Delnice, where several tens of thousands of guns and ammunition were destroyed on that occasion in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So -- but you cannot estimate how many weapons you got back?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: It would be my assessment that it was between 60 and 70 per cent of the weapons of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to the weapons that you -- that were seized during the war as such, I would like to put to you a quote from tab 3. Tab 3, new exhibit. And it's actually a reference, it's in English, and therefore I quote it. I'll read it to you. It's a reference to a lecture given by General Tus in -- 7th of February, 1993, and in relation to the Croatian army, he says the following: "By 1 October 1991, 24 brigades had been formed and another ten were being established. Near the end of that year, the Croatian army had already grown to about 200 fighting men in six zones of operations with 63 brigades and a navy, air force, and air defence. Is that also what you would say?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That was right with respect to the number of brigades. First of all, these 24 brigades up until the 1st of October 1991, but not as far as their weapons were concerned, because part of the brigades at the time, regardless of the fact that they had been mobilised were -- either had no weapons at all or only half the number had the weapons required by the beginning of October. By the end of the year, the -- there were about 63 brigades, and they were fully armed by that time in the way that I mentioned a moment ago, which means in part through the weapons given back by the Territorial Defence and in part by taking over the JNA barracks on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. And I have to stress here that -- I apologise. Yes? I would like to emphasise that it was said in the translation that 63 brigades including the air force and navy, which means there are around 63 brigades for the ground forces and the air force and navy were also formed, although truth to tell, they weren't armed properly at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is also a reference in this same article from General Tus saying that general mobilisation was not declared in Croatia because there were not enough weapons for everyone. Is that also your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The general mobilisation was to have been declared already at the beginning of September, but it was not because there wasn't enough -- there weren't enough weapons to go around.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to the weapons seized during the takeover of garrisons, he also remarks that in this way, "We captured 230 tanks, more than 400 heavy artillery pieces, coastal artillery, several warships and a large amount of light weapons." Would you also agree to this?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, with the proviso that these 230 tanks also refers to armoured personnel carriers, APCs, and the basic source was the Varazdin Corps which surrendered in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These entire weapons seized, in which time period were these weapons seized? You already mentioned September 1991. How long did this process take place?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The first operations to take over the weapons depots started at the end of August, 1991, and went on until roughly the beginning of the negotiations with the JNA about a peaceful withdrawal, which means sometime around the 10th of October, 1991, as far as the taking over of the barracks is concerned. But the process of taking over the Territorial Defence weapons went on until the end of the year, as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did -- when the JNA left the barracks in that 70 per cent of the territory, did they also leave equipment and weapons behind that you then could take over?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Except for equipment and weapons or, rather, part of the equipment and weapons belonging to the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia, they took all weaponry and equipment. The part they were not able to take away they left in such a state that it wasn't operational. It couldn't be used. And that was also the result of The Hague agreement by which the JNA had to withdraw from the Republic of Croatia taking weapons and equipment with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You worked in the security administration in the JNA for how many years?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I worked in the security service. As to the security administration, I did not work in that body. However, all the security -- JNA security organs headed by the security administration is incorporated under the JNA security service, and it is the JNA security service in which I worked from June 1971 until the beginning of March 1991, when I was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness Exhibit 387, and that is actually in this green bundle, tab 36. We have here a chart of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do not need to have you explain it. I just would like you to tell the Judges in which position you were when you left. Could you tell us exactly where you were positioned?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I was positioned as chief of security of the 5th Air Force Corps, which is here. It is within the composition of the RV and PVO security department in air force and air defence, and it is the last box on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It's where we have the number five?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: My superior in the security service was the chief of the security administration of the air force, organ of the air force and anti-air defence in Zemun, and that was Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is enough in relation to the chart. I have just a few questions in relation to the chain of command within the security organs. Officers in the security organs of the JNA, were they part of two chains of reporting and command, and what were the chains?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: All the members of the corresponding units or commands in the former JNA were under a unified command of a commander, right up to the top and the federal secretary for national defence. There was a single command. However, the security organs had their own parallel, professional chain of command, control and command, which means that a part of the duties and assignments they had, which were purely counter-intelligence or, for example, of a professional nature, they were responsible exclusively to their professional leader down that chain of command or up the chain of control and command. And the other tasks such as prevention, protection of confidentiality and so on, for that they were accountable to their military commanders. So that is that double chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could General Vasiljevic, as the head of the security administration or the SSNO, General Kadijevic, could they issue orders down the security chain of command without informing the immediate Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. military commanders involved?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic could do so in view of the chain of command for the security service. However, in the spirit of the guidelines given by the military commander, in this case the federal secretary for national defence. What I mean is this: The federal secretary for national defence and the commanders of the military districts, including the air force and the navy, could be informed and as a rule were informed with all the details of the service's activities. So that for them in that field, in that domain, there should not have been any secrets.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Giving the -- now the reporting, in case a war crime had been committed, how would such an event be reported within the chain of command and reporting of the security organs? What would the officer, the security officer, have to do?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: In the JNA, there were several reporting chains as to the situation in any given unit. I can enumerate at least five of them. One line was the chain of command by which the lowest commander informs his superior officer about the situation or whenever an event takes place or gives a regular situation report. The second line is the political line, the political chain, including political organs. The third line or chain is the League of Communists of Yugoslavia chain, which at that time in the JNA, and I'm not talking about 1991 here any more because I don't know about that, but it had its chain of reporting. The fourth chain was the chain of the military police chain of reporting, and they reported to the military police in a professional manner to the very tops that were in the Federal Secretariat. And then there was a fifth chain of reporting which was the security chain of reporting, and they reported to their superior officers following directives and guidelines of the superior security organ and the chain of command itself. When an event took place in which a security officer considered that he ought to be engaged, involved, to clear up the problem that had occurred such as a war crime, if that had taken place or if there was some emergency in the region or in the formation, then he would contact his sources. That would mean that he would apply his regular methods. He would take stock of the situation and report back to the commander. He would tell him all the things he needed to know and take steps to deal with the situation that had occurred. And as to the overall subject, he would inform his superior in the service itself. So that was that involvement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned the political organs and the political chain. What do you mean? What do you mean within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: They were organs who were -- which were in the JNA, and they were very powerful. And they were in charge, basically, for moral guidance and morale boosting, morale boosting with fighters, with members of the formations and units to be able them to carry out their assignments and the orders that the unit had been given. These organs, then, were deployed and distributed from the bottom to the top, right throughout the former structure of the JNA. And it was their duty to report on the situations that affected the morale of the unit and its members.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it obligatory to inform the top levels of war crimes happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Certainly that obligation did exist, because the top level had to be informed and reported to, and it was, at least in peacetime, and that is the time that I am acquainted with in the JNA. They had to inform on the most minute incident that took place, either in a unit or in the region where the unit was deployed at the time. As to any mass deaths, how they occurred is another matter, but, yes, that certainly had to be the subject of the reporting right up to the top levels of the JNA, top echelons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put to you now several documents related to reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if that would be a convenient time. It's half past ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General Agotic, we are now going to adjourn for 20 minutes. I must tell you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- As we tell all the witnesses not to speak to anybody until your evidence is over about it, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, first I would like to turn to a report of Major Branislav Ristic from the 27th of November, 1991, related to the killing of civilians in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Exhibit 387, tab 34 from the green bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I don't want you to comment on what is actually written in the report, just the following: Is this a report of a security organ officer to another higher ranking security organ?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And according to your experience, is it an authentic report?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I can say that the security organs did write reports of this kind with respect to the rules of service for the security organs that provided for this kind of report to be written and compiled, and I do believe that it is authentic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it says here it goes to the 9th Corps. Is that the Knin Corps?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. The corps command in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the next tab, that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's tab 387 -- sorry, Exhibit 387, tab 35.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's now a report of the 1st of December, 1991, from a Lieutenant Radjen, to the authorised military police official in Benkovac. Would that be a report within this military chain, military police chain, that you mentioned earlier on?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes. This quite obviously is a man having the rank of commander, platoon commander who went to the village of Skabrnja after the massacre had been committed to ascertain the situation on the ground, and in this way he reports to his superior officer in the military police and informs him of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it authentic according to your knowledge of the procedures?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I think it is authentic. That's how it is written and that's how it was done essentially in the military police service, how these things were done.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next is tab 4. This is now a new exhibit, Your Honours, tab 4 of the Exhibit 475. This is now a report also related to Skabrnja and Nadin. It's Lieutenant Commander Rosic reporting to the 9th Corps security organ on the 8th of March, 1992. Is that an authentic document within the security organs line of reporting and command?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This Official Note is the old form that was still used until the 1990s in the security service. However, it was -- it was used and documents were written according to this principle. So I think that it was compiled and written at the time it says it was with the purpose it was written as it says in this official report.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This -- this document and also some others are not signed by the -- by the security officer. Is that something extraordinary or was that rather usually so?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: It was usual, customary, and it wasn't signed. Official reports weren't signed, or this kind of note on applying the methods of work that we saw a moment ago. So that was customary, usual, yes, in the service. The source or, rather, the person who compiled the document would state in the upper left-hand corner this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next is tab 5. It's a -- again a document within the security organs, and it goes to the 9th Corps, and it relates now to an event in Bruska, and it's of the 11th of March, 1992. Is this an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The same as the previous one. I do believe it is authentic, yes, because that was the type of form it would take in the service. So it's a report once again to the superior officer in the security organ of the command of the 9th Corps of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to refer you in this -- in regard of this report, I would like to refer you to the end of the report. There is a remark made. It says: "As much as I know, SRS police station Benkovac has completed its investigation in this case, making a conclusion that for this massacre should be held responsible Ustasha sabotage terrorist group. I believe that they did not have material evidence in order to make such conclusion and that the investigation in this case should be reopened for the purpose of taking the blame for the massacre of Serb nation." Are you aware -- were you aware that this was tried, to blame the Croats for this?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I did hear that there was manipulation and that this particular case in Grusun [phoen] was ascribed to the Croatian side, that from our information later on, which gave a review of the situation on occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia, they wrote about this. That's what was written at the time. And obviously, the security organs of the JNA had a different conclusion, made a different conclusion about that same event than was presented by the police station or public security station of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the next document, tab 6, it's again a security organ's notes related to Bruska, and it's from Major Ristic and going to the 9th Corps. Is that an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, authentic, just like the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The last -- the last one in this context is tab 7, and it's a report, a situation report, from Lieutenant Colonel Slobodan Tarbuk of the 13th of July, 1991 to the security organs of the 5th Military District and the 10th corps. First of all, Lieutenant Colonel Tarbuk, do you know this person and his position?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him from those days during peacetime. He was one of the organs of security in the 5th Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this is an urgent security report, and it refers to an attack on the Kraljevcani police. Is that a Croatian police station in that place?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's right. Yes, it is the Croatian police station and it's a place in Banija not far from the town of Sisak. And this particular document is a telegram or as we used to call it in the JNA a dispatch which informed urgently, gave information urgently about a particular event. And after it, it should have been accompanied by the kind of document that we saw in the first example, first exhibit. It should have taken that form containing more details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in this document, reference is made in the first paragraph and also in the last paragraph to special unit commander Dusan Momcilovic, and there's also in the last paragraph mentioned special forces from Knin. Were these JNA forces or something different or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: As for this Dusan Momcilovic, I don't know him. I didn't hear of him before. And in this last paragraph it says that 24 persons came from the special unit training in Knin. They had spent three weeks there, and they were immediately sent to the area where they were used for combat purposes. It is obvious that these are members of special forces of the so-called SAO Krajina at that time, not members of the special forces of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in that last paragraph is also a reference to -- that they were immediately sent to Samarica. Samarica, was there a military base there, and if so, who was in control?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was in charge, but I know that in Samarica there was the command of a unit that was at the level of a brigade. It existed there throughout the war all the way up to Operation Storm in 1995. Actually, this is a hilly area, a forested, and it is well suited to special operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That should be enough for this document. We don't need to go into the details. Now, this is an urgent situation report. In the war situation in 1991, would the security administration submit daily reports, weekly reports, monthly reports? Can you explain that, what they actually reported and which frequencies? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: In the military organisation, in principle, reporting concerning certain events takes place once these events had happened. This form of reporting such as telegrams are or sometimes there are even voice messages involved, that is to say telephones or radio links. This means that a superior is informed by his subordinate immediately upon learning about a certain event. However, in all orders related to activities during the day or in a particular stage that may involve a longer period of time, it is stated and for the most part this is done in the last paragraph of the order, it says "Reporting," and for the most part it is the following wording, and I believe that in the JNA, from the summer of 1991 when I left, this was not changed, and this is how it read: "Daily reporting," up to such-and-such hour. For lower-level units earlier, and for higher-level units later, so that all these reports could be compiled in time, regularly on a daily basis. If there is an emergency, then reporting should be immediate. I believe that that was JNA practice during the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before the war, did the security organs monitor nationalist movements including Serbian nationalism?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. Security organs throughout the period of my service, and that is almost all of 20 years, were in charge of acting vis-a-vis the so-called internal enemy. At that time, that's what it was called, the structure that opposed the government or the system. One of the main structures, from 1971 onwards, that is to say from when I joined the service and all the way up to the end, was viewing nationalist tendencies or occurrences in the JNA. When speaking of nationalist occurrences, it was not specified which occurrences these actually were. This had to do with all nationalisms, depending on which one was topical at a given point in time. Then more attention was focused on that particular form of nationalism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt, but if counsel wants something elucidated, she can always ask. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask request you to be more brief in your answers and just answer the question that I actually put. Now did the JNA leadership react to Serb nationalism? Did they oppose it as well?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: They were against Serb nationalism in the time that went all the way up to the end of 1989, the beginning of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were nationalist officers actually placed under surveillance, and if so, can you give an example?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: They were actually placed under surveillance, yes. I'm going to give an example that I'm aware of from the air force. That is General Mika Stevanovic. The security service of the JNA decided to place him under surveillance because he was in favour of Serbian nationalism, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did this affect his career negatively or was he later on promoted?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This affected his career negatively until the beginning of the war. However, during the war, he was promoted to the position of commander of the air force, that is to say, it was no longer viewed as a disadvantage on his part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does this mean the JNA changed their policy towards Serb nationalism at some point in time, and if so, when and why?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Obviously during the war it was changed. In the JNA, through information that regularly came in from Belgrade from the political administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, tasks were given to all units and also all members of the JNA were informed that Yugoslavia had to be preserved at all costs.
