My assessment and the assessment of people who were around me then and later was that the JNA accepted the option favoured by the Serb leadership, that is to say to preserve Yugoslavia at all costs, either Yugoslavia in its entirety or in an abridged form.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the League of Communists of Yugoslavia disintegrated in 1990, was a League of Communist Movement for Yugoslavia formed and supported by the JNA leadership?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did they have this same aim, that is, preservation of Yugoslavia at all costs as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. The League of Communist Movement for Yugoslavia was established towards the end of 1990. The army leadership was in favour of the League of Communist Movement for Yugoslavia. Until the 15th of January, 1991, all members of the JNA were supposed to decide whether they are going to become members of the League of Communist Movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those who did not join the movement, did they suffer any disadvantages within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. They were at a disadvantage because they were immediately viewed with mistrust, and whenever the opportunity arose, they were removed from positions of greater responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you removed, and if so, who replaced you?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I openly spoke against the movement, and I did not wish to join it. When the first opportunity arose to replace me, this was the 1st of March, 1991, and that is indeed when I was replaced by my superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who replaced you?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Jovo Topalovic, my deputy until then, was appointed to the position that I had held.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is a Serb from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said the first opportunity was taken to replace you. What was the -- actually the reason to replace you on the 2nd of March, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: No reason was referred to in writing. However, the pretext was my assessment of what had happened in Pakrac on the 1st of March, 1991, and the role of the JNA in these developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which way did you disagree with what happened there? What was in dispute between you and your superior on this point?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I was in favour of the following: That the newly-elected leaderships of the republics, in this case Slovenia and Croatia, and this is the area where I was operating together with my corps, had to be recognised. Also, that they were legally elected at multi-party elections. My superiors held such views against me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you said that you were replaced on the 2nd of March but you, however, stayed in the JNA until July, what did you do? What kind of tasks did you have in that time in between?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Formally, it was called being at the disposal of the command of the 5th Corps of the air force and the anti-aircraft units and the air defence. Actually, I was assigned an office where I did not sit. I came to work, and I was not given any assignments whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you take part in briefings and discussions during this time?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I did not take part in any official meetings, and I was not invited to any. I only speak to people who came to see me or people I happened to come across. But as for the official line of command vis-a-vis myself, there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were other non-Serbs or opponents to the JNA official policy, were they also replaced in the security organs in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: During the first half of 1991, no prominent members of the service were replaced because until then, the service had already been cleansed sufficiently of all those who did not agree with the JNA line or the League of Communist movement in Yugoslavia line.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the security or administration pre -- or rather, homogenous Serb-Montenegrin staff? At that time. I'm speaking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. In 1991, it had practically a nationally homogenous composition of members of the Serb and Montenegrin ethnic groups only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was this structure used for passing sensitive orders through the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of orders? If you know.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: For example, the arming of Serb areas in the Republic of Croatia went through that line. From the end of 1990 until the beginning of the war while I was in a position to follow this or to be informed about it in part at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We will come to some of the details of this later on. Was the security administration or the organs an important factor in relation to appointments of JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: They were. The security administration or, rather, the security organ had the possibility of vetoing an appointment or at least raising objections in respect of an officer who was supposed to be appointed to a particular post.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned the JNA goal of the preservation of Yugoslavia at all costs. Was there a plan how to achieve that in relation to the governments in Slovenia and Croatia, and if so, did this plan evolve?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: There was such a plan, and it was corrected, modified depending on how the situation evolved. At first the plan was to preserve Yugoslavia at all costs. I know that in the month of June 1990, General Adzic, at that time chief of the General Staff of the JNA, at a meeting with part of the military commanders at the Zagreb airport, Pleso, he then said in response to a question put by a general, a Serb in this case, how to cooperate in the future with the new authorities in the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia. Adzic spoke very energetically and in a very angry manner, "There is no cooperation with Tudjman. Tudjman should be told vamoose from that chair." That meant that he would not recognise the legal -- legally elected authorities of Croatia. Later on, the preparations of the JNA did develop along that course as Serbs were armed in that part of Croatia, because it was expected that with JNA support, they would be the force that would overthrow the Croatian leadership. Later on in 1991, as the situation developed in the territory of Croatia, this plan was modified due to pressure exerted by international factors. After the war, after it left Yugoslavia, after Slovenia left Yugoslavia, then Croatia was next. Croatia was supposed to be placed under the control of the JNA, all of it. This was the plan that was in existence until the second half of 1991. Later on, it was modified as well. I used to call it Plan B. Croatia was supposed to be placed under control up to the Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag line, and that was supposed to include territories that had majority Serb populations, but also they included a considerable part of other Croatian territories. Subsequently, even that plan was modified, and then Plan C was opted for. This plan meant that the JNA, along with Serb insurgents, would take the territory that were predominantly inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As for Plan A, the toppling, as I understand you, the overthrowing of the Croatian government, did you ever see any plan or any document or any preparation to do that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I was at too low a level at that time in order to be in a position to see that plan. Whether it existed as such on paper is something that I don't know. However, all information that came in from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, either along the line of the political administration or along the line of the security administration, indicated such options. The only thing I saw was a document that wished to carry through a plan to take the borders of Croatia in a certain form. This was Plan A. And this was from September 1991, and it was sent to units in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. It was sent by the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did you see this document? You said you saw it, but you were no more in the JNA. So how did you see it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This document was in the form of a telegram on several pages, and it arrived from the General Staff to the signals brigade in Samobor. These particular barracks were taken by the Croatian army during the month of September, and at that time, this document was seized. They found that document in their archives, and that's how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were not in a position to locate this document. We have asked -- we had asked the witness to look for it, but he didn't find it, he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness can tell more detail about the contents of the document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, if you remember? What was requested or said in this document?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: In this document, assignments were given to JNA units in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, namely that in concert with forces that got close to the borders of the Republic of Croatia from Bosnia and from Serbia, namely Vojvodina and also Montenegro, that the territory of the Republic of Croatia should be cut, so to speak, in various directions. Appropriate operations should take place on the part of units that were already in the Republic of Croatia and the newly arrived units from other republics, and that is how the borders of Croatia should be taken. This order specifically refers to the border with Slovenia. There is specific reference to the following direction: From Knin towards Zadar, that this is where the territory of Croatia should be cut. Then also the Neretva valley, the Neretva River valley. This was basically the content of this telegram that was seized in the month of September. In that document, there is no reference to an overthrow of the government of the Republic of Croatia because this is a military order. It talks about taking the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and this, in other words, means that the new government should be gotten rid of. That is what I'd have to say at this point, and if necessary, I can talk about it in greater detail too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think we actually come to this -- these directions in a different way when we speak about the book of Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Or would Your Honour Judge Kwon like to have more details?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me refer you now to two documents, two quotes from a book of Jovica Jovic -- sorry. Jovica. Mr. Jovic, the then president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you'll need to take care about this. I'm not quite sure on what basis this is being put in. Mr. Kay, perhaps you'd like to address us on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I've been looking through the exhibits that have come this morning with this particular witness, and I notice there's General Kadijevic's book further along in the testimony. I know the Trial Chamber has been very concerned that we're not introducing material that is the opinions of other people and using witnesses to thereby adopt it without them giving their own testimony on the matter. It's an artificial form, if you like, of putting evidence before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it's admissible. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, this is what Mr. Jovic writes. If you want to call him, you can, but I'm not quite sure how the witness can deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness had actually explained the plan, how he saw it develop and evolve over this time period of about a year, and I actually wanted to put only the quotes to him, a few quotes to him related to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Then ask him if he agrees with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Only if that is what he saw happening on the ground. That is what I wanted to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can tell us what he saw happening, of course. That's his evidence. But he can't use Jovic's book or anybody else's book to say that is what he saw happening. If you want him to give evidence about what he saw, he must give it yourself, not use somebody else's opinions, which are those people's opinions and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I will skip the book, but the witness had prepared a map related to operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Have we admitted Jovic's diary already?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It was actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Marked under --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 448.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Only portions actually where witnesses had a close relation to the book and the sequences described in the book. When a certain event was described in Jovic's book where a witness was mentioned or related to, then it was admitted in a very few sections. The situation here would be different, of course, because the witness wasn't addressed here in any relation to the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put to the witness now a map with marks on it. It would be exhibit from the Croatian map binder. It's Exhibit 326, tab 30, and -- Your Honours, you have this map at the end of the green -- it's in a separate -- you have it already. It's a separate map binder, and you can see certain troop movements here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My question to you, General, is did you mark this map, and what is the basis of these markings?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did mark the map. The places marked here and, globally speaking, that was the implementation of the order that I mentioned a moment ago, and that was by making a breakthrough and taking control of Eastern Slavonia, and with the assistance of the Serb population in the western part of Slavonia, this is this yellow line from Nova Gradiska to Virovitica which was slightly more to the west, left of that line, in those days that area was already under the control of Serb rebels. So by a fast operation from Eastern Slavonia, using a Guards Unit which was brought there from Belgrade, that it should link up with these other forces in Western Slavonia, and together with surrounded units in the region of Varazdin, Bjelovar, and Zagreb, Karlovac, that they should reach the border between Croatia and Slovenia. Another part of the forces from the region of Bihac, which at that time was already under the control of the Serb insurgents, that it should head towards Karlovac to facilitate the realisation of the task I have just described and a third part of this task was for forces from Knin, and with units brought from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the territory should be -- a line should be drawn towards the town of Zadar. A fourth part of that task was to use units from the region of Mostar to make a breakthrough towards Split and there to cut the Republic of Croatia. That was, in general terms, the order. Mention was also made about units from the region of Trebinje, that is Eastern Herzegovina, and units from Montenegro that should also be deployed to surround Dubrovnik, to place it under a blockade, to reach the Neretva River valley, which is right here, in the area of Metkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that this was the original plan, and it was not executed in this way then. Why not? Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand the plan. It's extremely complicated. Can you just put it in a few words for us, General, so we can understand it? What was the plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The plan, in global terms, was to take control of the territory of the Republic of Croatia north of the Sava River and south of the Sava as far as the Kupa River, to reach the border between the Republic of Croatia and Slovenia. So all the territory between the Drava and the Sava should have been taken control of by JNA units. This was one part of it. The second was to cut the territory of the Republic of Croatia in two between Knin and Zadar so as to prevent communication between those two parts. And this part of the task was the only part that was actually implemented. And the fourth part was to intersect it again between Mostar and Split, so that the Republic of Croatia as a whole could not communicate within its own territory. And the fifth part was achieved, that is, Dubrovnik was placed under a blockade using units from Trebinje and Montenegro. But it wasn't fully implemented for reasons I will explain later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we must really try and speed this up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have already mentioned that the plan was later modified and reduced to parts of Croatia. And do you know whether this -- on what these modifications were based? Was it the resistance of the Croatian forces, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: There were two reasons. The first and main reason was the resistance of the Croatian forces. The second reason was the inability of JNA units to achieve it, because they were unable to mobilise forces where they wanted to mobilise forces, that is, to replenish their units. They didn't have sufficient manpower. And a third reason, I don't know how important it is, that was the pressure of the international public opinion to put an end to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that the JNA security organs were involved in the arming of Croatian Serbs. Who did that? Which part of the security organs and how do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I know that this was done by the 2nd Detachment of the counter-intelligence group. It was a section that was based in Zagreb, a brigade in which I worked too. And I heard this from members of that same detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: To be specific, from the then-Lieutenant Colonel Mirko Martic who was chief of that detachment. And later on, upon joining the Croatian army, I heard it from then-Major Slavko Hodak -- Rakaric, who was at the airport in Bihac, and Major Stjepan Rakaric, who was a member of the same 2nd Detachment of the counter-intelligence group. Secondly, I also know that during the spring of 1991, two members of the security organ, one of them is Lieutenant Colonel Smiljanic from the 5th Military District was apprehended by the Croatian police in Eastern Slavonia together with a truck full of light weapons which they had been distributing to the Serb population in those villages. And this was reported on by the Croatian press at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you speak about the arming of the Croatian Serbs, in which time period was that done from the -- by the security organs? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This was the autumn of 1990 and the spring of 1991. Whether it was done later on, I don't know, but I can guarantee as regards this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in which region did that take place?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Detachment of the counter-intelligence group was responsible for the regions of Banija, Kordun, and the Bihac Krajina or the area around Bihac, the Serb villages around Bihac. And the part in Eastern Slavonia was under the 5th Military District that was headquartered in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You meaning that had Mirko Martic was actually the head of this organisation, the 2nd KOG detachment that did it. Did he get an order to do so or was it his random action?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he received an order from his superior Colonel Rakocevic. Now, whether people above Rakocevic in the service were aware of this I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the security organs have weapons storage themselves or would they get the weapons from other parts of the JNA or even elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The security service did not have its own storage space. The warehouses were under military commanders, and the 2nd Detachment of the KOG used the warehouse at the Bihac airport to arm these elements that I have referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean that they needed cooperation from the military commanders responsible for the warehouses?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. They needed cooperation, and they probably encountered a positive opinion from that particular commander regarding those activities and were given those weapons by him. Now, whether he received any order along any chain of command, I don't know. Probably he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the Bihac airport JNA base, did you get information that they also had a detention facility there?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I did have information to that effect in the village of Valjevac, in the immediate vicinity of the Bihac airport. One could even say that it was within that compound of the air base.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Judges about the fate of the priest Josip Bogovic and how you met him?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Josip Bogovic was a priest in the area right next to Bihac, in the village of Drezni Grad and he was arrested by JNA security organs sometime in September 1991 because he had authority in the area. And he was sent to that reception centre at the Bihac airport, and after some time, he was sent on to the Batajnica airport and kept in detention for several months. He was interrogated and mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you interview this person or did you speak to this person after his release and were you actually involved in efforts to get him released?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: As a negotiator on behalf of the Croatian government with the JNA, having learnt that he had been arrested, at those negotiations with General Raseta, I requested that he be released. And when he was released several months later, he contacted me and I had a talk with him about the circumstances of his detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you notice any physical or mental results of his detention on him?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The man was psychologically in a bad condition, and I -- to this day he has problems, and I believe that these were provoked by that detention. I didn't see any physical injuries, nor did I examine him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned already that you were negotiating with General Raseta. Were you indeed in 1991 one of the chief negotiators of the Croatian side in negotiations with the Serb -- the JNA and the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was appointed by the president of the Republic as the authorised negotiator with the JNA regarding their withdrawal from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did the negotiations start?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The negotiations started on the 8th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where did they take place and how often? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The talks took place at the Hotel I in Zagreb with the mediation of monitors from the European Community, and they were held on a daily basis up until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was General Raseta the chief negotiator on the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: His superior, in the formal sense, was the commander of the 5th Military District, Colonel General Zivota Avramovic, who was the commander in Zagreb. At the time of the negotiations, he had been withdrawn together with his command to the area of Slunj. And the consultant during the negotiations was most frequently Admiral Brovet. He would pass on the positions to him. He would advise him. And to some extent General Adzic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean that General Raseta was in frequent contact with the JNA headquarters in Belgrade, that's Brovet and Adzic?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: He would most frequently consult with Admiral Brovet, and he did so several times a day and almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Because we were sitting at the opposite ends of the table. And whenever I insisted on something, there would be a break in the negotiations. He would go to the room next door. He would make a telephone call, speak to Brovet or Adzic, and then he would come back with his position. And very frequently he would even mention the names of the people he had consulted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he in contact with Zivota -- General Zivota Panic as well?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: On one occasion he was, I am quite sure, in contact with General Zivota Panic, and that was with respect to the siege of Vukovar and the shelling of the hospital in Vukovar. I protested against it and requested that it stop. And after consulting, after his consultations, he came back and said that he had spoken to General Zivota Panic, the commander of the Belgrade Military District who, at the observation post near Vukovar, who was there and who said that the Croatian side was lying, that the hospital was not being hit --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just listen to the questions. Yes. Are we going on now to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We are actually going through the documents, starting at tab 8 in relation to notice, when complaints were made and how it was reacted to. It's actually the end of the summary when you look at the proofing summary. It's Vukovar. It's actually the negotiations between the Croats and the JNA including Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to put -- first, you haven't mentioned when that -- on what date Panic was according to what was said in Vukovar and the shelling of the hospital. When was that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: It was in October 1991, in the third decade of that month. I have it noted down in my diary, but I can't recollect the exact date now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First of all, have a look at tab 8. That's the memorandum, and that's the memorandum of 8 October 1991. That's the initial agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in point 1 in this memorandum, there is the general cease-fire mentioned. Was the -- was it followed by subsequent cease-fires agreed upon during the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then at point 3, there is a mention of the simultaneous lifting of the blockade and the withdrawal of the JNA. How many months did it last and what were the main obstacles from your side?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The negotiations and the withdrawal of the JNA lasted on the whole until the end of 1991, but some smaller units on the islands of Vis and Lastovo left at the end of 1992. The main problem in this connection was that JNA units wanted to take with them the entire armaments and equipment for which they needed additional means of transport. And we spent most of the time at the negotiations discussing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also have a -- the Croatian side, did you also have a special request on the order of the withdrawal that was opposed by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I insisted on two points. First, that the JNA units should withdraw, which did not have their peacetime garrisons in Croatia. That is, they were brought there for the needs of the war. And secondly, I insisted that the topic of discussion should be the withdrawal of all JNA units from the territory of the whole of Croatia and not only from the part that was under the control of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to go into a few questions in relation to protests during negotiations. Did you protest against actions of the JNA or other Serb forces during these months of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: On a daily basis and several times during one day I did protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What would the ECMM observer do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The protests were in writing and oral ones, and the ECMM, at the time, asked to get a response from the JNA representative.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what -- how would Raseta react? What would he do?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Most frequently, he would say that what the Croatian side alleged was not true but that what was actually happening was quite the reverse, the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's now move to some of the documents related to such protests. And first, tab 9 related to the shelling of Dubrovnik, and it's a letter that you wrote to the ECMM on October 24, 1991. Had Dubrovnik been shelled at that time, and what did follow your protest, your written protest this time?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This is my protest, yes. Dubrovnik had been shelled at the time. And after that, Raseta's response was, as far as I remember, to say that that was not correct, that the Croatian forces were just feigning attacks, especially on the old, protected city area of Dubrovnik, the old town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next -- the next document is actually an exhibit that is already provided. That means it is in the green bundle. It's Exhibit 330, tab 12, and it is Minister Ivan Vekic writing to the SFRY committee for control of the truce, and he's referring to attacks in the Osijek region. Do you know what the response was to this protest or request, rather, for urgent intervention?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the answer given was, but I do know that these particular villages, two months later, were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever protest any expulsion of Croats?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. I did so on a daily basis in the course of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what would be General Raseta's response to that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: His response would be that he would see what it was about. He would inquire. And he said that people were leaving of their own free will and that there was no pressure that was being brought to bear against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: According to your information, was that what was really happening?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: No, that was not what was really happening, because all the villages -- actually, it was tactics well known in Eastern Slavonia, that is to say before attacking the villages, they would be heavily shelled first, and the people under pressure of this kind left the area from the front. And on occupied territories, there were constant pressures being exerted by the new Serb authorities to prevail upon the Croatian population to leave and this was realised.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have put to the witness now the tab numbers 10 to 17. They all relate to Vukovar. And the situation in Vukovar, as it can be seen, is discussed right from the beginning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as we can see, we have now tab 10, October the 12th, and it's a letter from you to the ECMM, and it is -- refers to the wounded, the wounded in Vukovar. Was that a constant concern and was that constantly raised during the negotiations with General Raseta?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That was a constant problem, and most of the negotiations were taken up with discussing the problem of Vukovar especially the sick and wounded from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 11 is a letter about the 18th of October, 1991. It's from General Tus, and it's also referring to artillery attacks and wounded persons. Is that an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And now the next, tab 12. We have here a document related to a proposal dated the 17th of November, 1991. Is that what was agreed with regard to the evacuation of the sick and wounded from Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: During the time immediately prior to the occupation of Vukovar, the main negotiations on the evacuation of the sick and wounded was initiated by the Minister of Health, Dr. Andrija Hebrang. And I remember this document. It did exist at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it was agreed to have an evacuation in a certain -- around -- along a certain route on the 7th -- 17th of November. And if you turn to tab 13, there is actually an agreement of the 18th of November in relation to such an evacuation. And can you tell us who signs it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This agreement was signed on the Croatian side by Dr. Andrija Hebrang, and for the JNA it was signed by General Andrija Raseta.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In point 6 of this agreement, it actually refers to the Republic of Croatia and the JNA will recognise the neutrality of the Vukovar Hospital during a period governing the evacuation. Did the JNA keep that? Did they comply with this fact?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The JNA did not comply, and this can be seen fully today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have in fact, had evidence about that, and I think we've had this document in evidence. If you look at the evidence of Dr. Bosanac, I think we covered this document. We've certainly seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next document in this row is tab 14. We have here Raseta, General Raseta, making a proposal for the -- on the 21st of November, and it refers to a verbal agreement reached on the 20th. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when we look at tab 15, it's actually a letter from you directed to Raseta, also referring to that same verbal agreement. There is a point where the transfer from the wounded and sick was supposed to take place Bosanska Raca. We know already, and we do not need to discuss that. Only some of the people actually reached this place. What did you do when you noticed that only some of the people had arrived there?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: There were daily protests to the JNA via General Raseta to the effect that the remaining number of wounded and those who were evacuated should be sent along that route or some other route to the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the response? What was said?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The response was to say, "We don't know where they are. It will take place. Wait. We will organise it." But more or less indeterminate. And we didn't have anyway to force them to behave differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then we have actually the tab 16 and tab 17, letters of Granic, Dr. Granic, and Minister Hebrang asking for where the wounded are and the missing people are. Did the JNA ever tell you or did you find out otherwise?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever get an official response from the JNA about what happened to the missing people?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Never. We never received an official written response from the JNA. Not even an oral one, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it's past that time. Would that be a convenient moment or do you want a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. No, Vukovar is covered. I would just want to speak about a different point, the expulsion of people and the complaints of people about that, yes, and Saborsko. I would address Saborsko briefly with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, tab 18 is an information on a meeting of the head of mission of the ECMM and Prime Minister Granic of the 15th of January, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 1992, and you are also mentioned as participant in these talks. Was this a preparatory meeting for future negotiations with Raseta?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon the completion of this meeting in Zagreb, negotiations were later started in Hungary, and this was one of the agreements reached with the European Commission regarding such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's an English document but you had time to review it with an interpreter during the preparation of your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In point 4 of this information there are listed the Croatian priorities for the future talks and it says here under 4A. "To halt the process of intimidation of Croatians out of their homes and areas under JNA control as well as to halt their replacement by Serbian settlers." Can you tell us to which regions this refers? Where did this happen, and when?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: In all the occupied areas, people were moved out, which means in the eastern part, less so in the western part because it had already been cleansed of Croats earlier on, and in the Sector North and Sector South. But first and foremost in Sector East there were most such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that means Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And tab 19 is a letter -- rather, a fax, as you can see on the original, of the 15th of March, 1992. Is that an example of this sort of conduct, in this case related to the village of Boksic?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in this document, is that your handwriting, this handwritten note saying, "I have asked for the urgent sending of ECMM team from Belgrade for the purpose of protection of inhabitants ..."? Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And could the ECMM, then, access the region and could they stop what was going on?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: They should have had access from Belgrade. They didn't have access from Zagreb. I know that. And they could intervene. Now, whether they could stop it, obviously they couldn't because it continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did it continue? I mean, in the entire regions?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Up until the end of 1993, because by then all the areas taken control of by the Serbs had been cleansed by other -- of other ethnic groups. Only some old people remained in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then tab 20, it is a report, a summary of a series of meetings taking part on and around the 20th of March, 1992, between internationals and Croatians, tan says in paragraph 4 that you also took part in these talks, as did Mr. Ramljak, Ambassador Salgueiro, and also a Czech Consul-General. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was a whole series of such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as the document says, it's about expulsion of population and related issues. And in paragraph 2 in this document, it says as follows -- it refers first of all to the expulsion of 61 persons from Jovarnik and Nijemci. What kind of persons were expelled from there, ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: From Nijemci. Croats, because more than 95 per cent of the inhabitants were Croats before the war, whereas from Jovarnik and other areas in Eastern Slavonia members of other groups as well. To be more specific, Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks, who were quite numerous in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to quote something to you in relation to other ethnicities. It says here, "The Czech Consul-General had on 27 March come to complain, in strong language, over the expulsion of Czechs from Ilok. Ramljak, calling for a meeting ASAP which ECMM would also attend, strongly contended that the practice had developed in the UNPAs of attempted 'ethnic purge': - not only Croats, but Czechs, Hungarians, Ukrainians and Ruthenians were being driven out before UNPROFOR's deployment. Were you aware of this and to what time period does this refer?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That is correct. This did occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But when?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This was happening at the time. These were both individual cases and more large-scale cases. People would report it, and they were transferred to the Croatian side or brought as far as the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it says here in that same paragraph: "The worst areas were, at present, Central Dalmatia, Eastern Slavonia, and the Ilok region." Does that concur with your memory on the regions?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now, a different issue, and I will go now to a map, a map that refers to the attack on Saborsko, and it's actually a document that was marked for identification with another witness. It's tab -- Exhibit 326, tab 9. And the witness that actually was meant to use this document wasn't able to explain it, and I would like you, General, to help us. First of all, were you aware of what was going on in Saborsko on -- in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I was, because the president of the local commune in Saborsko would call me very frequently up until then asking for assistance in easing the pressure on Saborsko and the arming of Saborsko so that they might be able to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And is this a map, a -- is this a JNA map, according to your experience with that kind of maps?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: On this map, it doesn't say, as is customary. There should be a signature and the rank of the commander. But maps of this kind were made when planning any assault operations, offensive operations. So this is a map for the level of a brigade. And from what can be seen on it, it appears to be the map of the commander of the 5th Partisan Brigade that was stationed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The 5th Partisan Brigade, is that a JNA brigade or what kind of brigade is a Partisan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Partisan Brigades were envisaged in the process of mobilisation of the former JNA, and they were under the command of JNA units, and they were filled by the members of the local population who were under the obligation to serve in such brigades in defence. It was -- these Partisan Brigades were intended for the local territory, and they would not be deployed in other areas. They would be armed with light weapons, and they can defend the area and engage in small-scale offensive operations only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this red, the indications -- the red indications, would that be the Serb movements? And the blue ones, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The markings in red are those of the JNA and the Serbs, and the markings in blue are the Croatian forces in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And is this the attack on the -- an attack plan on Saborsko and the two other villages, Poljanac and --

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were you correct about the Croatian army being there? Were there any Croatian army units there or police units?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: There was a unit of the police there and the self-organised population of Saborsko, as well as the population of the villages up to Sertic Poljana, that is southeast from Saborsko towards the Plitvice lakes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And from this map, can you see the -- which units take part on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: First of all, I said that it was the 5th Partisan Brigade, that this was its map. And on her part, obviously, a tactical group had been formed from that Brigade. It is here called Tactical Group 2. And in Plasko which had been captured by Serb forces by then already, there was a company of Territorial Defence of Plasko, that here in the region of Ogrizovici north-west of Licka Jasenica and Saborsko, there was the 2nd armoured company -- battalion, I'm sorry, and in other positions there were some other smaller units. Also judging from the structure of the operation which is indicated here on the left-hand side, it can be seen that they had the support of the air force, from 8.40 until 9.10. Which means for half an hour they had air support. I assume that this came from Bihac air base, because at the time, it was active in combat and the planes were based at the Bihac airport. Also, we can see that artillery preparation and artillery support had been planned for that purpose. An artillery group of 122-millimetre howitzers which is a relatively large calibre from the region of the Plitvice lakes was positioned here. So this is not an operation of only members of the TO but also of the Partisan Brigade and legal units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many defenders were there? You mentioned police and you mentioned the local defenders. How many were there and what kind of weapons do they have?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I do not have the precise figures here, but there was one 100 men under arms on the outside in Saborsko and the surrounding villages. They were armed with light weapons, and that means rifles. And here in this presentation with the exception of some roadblocks by the Croatian side, there is no evidence that the attackers had envisaged any heavy artillery weapons here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know whether this plan was actually executed and -- executed according to this plan?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. This plan was executed, and Saborsko was captured, the people removed, and after that, it was completely razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether the defenders fled during the air force attack or the artillery that preceded the infantry attack?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Most of them -- most of the population fled, but the defenders withdrew in the face of a superior attacker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, help us. Where does this plan come from?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This plan was provided by the -- by the Croatian government. They seized it together with other documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you aware of this fact, General, that this document was seized?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this document, but I do know that many documents were seized after the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that the village, afterwards, was razed to the ground. Did that happen to other villages in that same region at about that same time? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: More or less all Croatian villages in this area were -- the people were displaced, after which the houses and all facilities were devastated. There were relatively few Croatian villages there in the area between Plitvice and Saborsko, but there were some in the area from Plitvice towards Slunj. But their occupation, the occupation of those villages, was carried out before that with the exception of Slunj itself. And I'm referring to the villages of Vaganac, Drezni Grad, and Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Agotic, in this map am I correct that there is a passage which refers to the casualties of this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot guarantee whether this was a forecast of casualties or whether they were actual casualties suffered, what we find here at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's the point I'd like to raise. It says -- according to the legend I was given earlier, red, three wounded, blue is around 315. Is it correct? Given that passage was this rather a report than a plan, if you have any observation on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would rather be a plan, because this figure of 315 can relate to the number of inhabitants in Saborsko, including those who were armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you can tell us the meaning of red and blues. Red, three wounded. That colour, three wounded, around 315. Three hundred and fifteen may be the number of inhabitants in your assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And it is a realistic assessment that there would be three wounded on the Serb side, because there was a disproportion in terms of armaments. And this figure of 315 were the people that were moved out of Saborsko, because that would roughly be the number of inhabitants it had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this context, I have also one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In a military map like this when you make such a plan, would you actually add a section like this, estimated -- estimated casualties for both sides?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This is usually included in the order. The map is an accompanying document and a component part of the order that is issued in written form, and one of the points is the estimated or assumed casualties. We do not have that written order. We only have the map. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this concludes the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I dropped the other map because it was not crucial and we are pressed for time. So it's the Slunj map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you provided very clear and precise answers, and I hope we will be able to make very efficient use of our time. First of all, I would like us to clear up a few matters that you commented on in the examination-in-chief towards the end of it. Namely I'm referring to the JNA plan for the preservation of Yugoslavia at all cost. You spoke about that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I gathered that when you were describing operations which the JNA had planned, the plan was to place the whole of Croatia under JNA control or, rather, for the forces to be positioned on the border towards Slovenia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was the first plan. I gather that you described this as the first plan that was elaborated. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you went on to explain how that plan was to be implemented, and you mentioned a dispatch of 1991, a telegram, in which this was elaborated in some detail. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have that cable, do we? But you are familiar with its contents.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But it is surely in the JNA archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We can probably obtain it, and I hope that there shouldn't be any real dispute over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the context of the assignment specified by that dispatch or cable, you speak about JNA forces being brought in from various areas and along different axes. In view of the fact that you are a general, a military expert therefore, could we clear up certain things that were explained in rather confused terms during some other testimony? So there is no dispute that the JNA had a plan to position itself on the border with Slovenia to preserve the SFRY, without Slovenia but including Croatia. Now, when you talk about axes of approach and the intersection of the territory, it's not a question of forming any kind of borders, as I understand you, but, rather, of cutting across the territory for bringing in units to fulfil this task of preserving the whole of Croatia within Yugoslavia by positioning the forces on the border with Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That is partially so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to that first plan, it reflected the JNA's intention to keep Croatia within the integral territory of the SFRY with the exception of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in view of that, when you mentioned forces being brought in from Bihac, Knin, the Neretva River valley, from the area of Montenegro, Serbia, et cetera, all that was part of the implementation process of that plan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this cutting of territory indicates the axes and directions along which the troops would come with a view to preserving Croatia within the borders of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Partially, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that, you go on to say that since that plan could not be implemented with success for the reasons that you gave that the assignment was reduced. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The second level of modification of that plan was to position the units along the line you mentioned, Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then after that, the third level of the further shrinking of the plan and the withdrawal of forces limited them to the territories where the Serbs had a majority, that is, the territories in which the population did not see the JNA as an enemy force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, from your explanations the first time here during the year and a half that this trial has been continuing, we can see for the first time now that these were military operations and no border that would go Karlovac, Virovitica, Karlobag?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That is partially true. Where the army positions itself that is where the border should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we're talking about a plan which the JNA had on the one hand and the Croatian armed forces on the other.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. They were two conflicting, opposing plans, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And throughout your testimony today, you ever made reference all the time to one side made up of the JNA and the other side made up of the armed forces of Croatia; right? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is there anywhere there do we see Serbia? Is Serbia anywhere there?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Whether it's there or not, I don't know. What I'm talking about is the situation on the ground that existed at the time. Now, who stood behind it, who was behind all this, that is up to others to prove. As a military man myself, that is how I saw it, and that is how I recount it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that that is why your testimony is very useful, because you as a soldier -- not only as a soldier but somebody who commanded the army and who was the main negotiator to boot on the other side you had the JNA as the negotiating party on the other side. That's right, isn't it, throughout the whole time?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as to the political leadership, as far as that is concerned, you spoke about the participation of President Tudjman when he attended SFRY meetings and the activities that went hand-in-hand with the activities that you testified about. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try and put some order into my questions and to make our work as efficacious as possible. From the very beginning, General, did you support the idea of an independent Croatian state outside the borders of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: What do you mean at the beginning? What beginning are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask it this way: When did you start supporting that idea as you were a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I lent my support to it from the moment when the war started on the territory of Croatia and when I realised that that was the only solution, that is to say, an independent Croatian state and all the other republics, in actual fact, the other republics of the former Yugoslavia. That applied to them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you described a moment ago the efforts made by the JNA, you reached the highest officer rank in the JNA. You were a colonel; right? And I'm sure you knew that the basic task of the JNA was to preserve Yugoslavia's integrity. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you, as a JNA officer yourself at that time, nonetheless one given moment changed your opinion and position and came to consider that it should not be preserved and that independent states should be set up in its stead.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it wasn't a moment in time. It was a process that I went through from 1989 onwards. In actual fact, I gave intensive thought to all this and wrote to General Veljko Kadijevic as the number one man in the former JNA. I wrote to him officially as the chief of security, in my official capacity, and I also wrote to him as a private individual. I don't know if he received those letters because I never got a response from him. But in those letters, I expressed my concern with regard to developments. From my level of vision, I was able to see that the relationships that prevailed were deteriorating and that they were leading up to a conflict on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and I also realised and saw that the JNA within this conflict or, rather, in preventing the conflict, to be more precise, could play a much more significant and effective role. And it could have done so had it not taken anybody's side. Had it sought for a peaceful solution or the reconstitution of Yugoslavia or a peaceful disassociation in Yugoslavia. But when all this fell through and when the JNA took one side over the others, and I can guarantee it was the Serb side that it took, it was at this point in time that I lost all hope in the JNA. And there was the war in Slovenia, and this was followed by the situation in Croatia. So that was the process. It wasn't a momentary decision. It was a process that led me to change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. But before your new career, the one you embarked upon, having spent your entire life as an officer of the JNA, you attended the military academy in Belgrade from which you graduated, you went to all the high military schools?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The War College as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The War College as the highest institution in the army?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a school attended by generals. And therefore, I also assume that you acquitted yourself affably in the JNA, and you were promoted with respect to rank and with respect to the highly important security position you held in the 5th Air Force Corps in which you stayed until March 1992; that is right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you spent most of your time in your career working on security matters, holding positions in the security sector?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as a professional man, as an expert, for officers who perform military security assignments and work in that field, do they appoint people that are highly respected, highly professional and in which they can place their trust? Of course along with all the military schools that you would have to have graduated from and everything else that officers have to have to occupy their positions. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that your main task as chief of the security command of the 5th Corps was to protect the units of that corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you mean by protection? What does "protection" imply? I assume that you feel you acquitted yourself affably and you did your work successfully; right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement, paragraph 6, you say that in fact, this entire security administration -- you don't have to look at your statement. I'm not going to play a trick on you or anything like that. I don't want to set a trap for you. You just went to enumerate neutral -- the neutralisation of the activities of foreign intelligence services, that that was one of your jobs and then to neutralise the work of extremists from emigres circles and to neutralise domestic or internal enemies; is that right? Those were the basic tasks that you had and you addressed them; right? Now, tell me, in what area did your -- were you engaged in most?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: From 1971, the service itself, right up until 1991, focused or, rather, 70 per cent of its capacities were focused on neutralising internal enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA as the sole legitimate armed force of the SFRY, was it against all forms of nationalism?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: For a time, yes, or, rather, during my years of service there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the situation in the SFRY after Tito's death became far more complex. That's right, isn't?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that it was immediately after his death that there was a burgeoning of different secessionists, separatists and other movements having elements of nationalistic extremism, chauvinism and the like which in one way or another posed a threat to Yugoslavia's integrity?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the security service carefully follow all these activities regardless of the side they came from, regardless of whether they were dealing with Serbs, Croats, Albanians, or whoever?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, for a time. Later on, it changed its position and attitude, and it no longer considered certain nationalisms to be dangerous, whereas it did consider others to be dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say certain nationalisms dangerous, others not, do you mean that it considered nationalisms to be dangerous who were geared towards the break-up of Yugoslavia, those?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: All nationalisms taken as a whole would, asserting their own ethnic group to the detriment of others, would come under that category, and this at the same time will lead to problems and the ultimate effect would be the break-up of Yugoslavia itself. Therefore, depending on the given period of time, the security service and administration would devote more or less attention to one or another nationalism depending on which it was. Whether this was historically justified or not, that's another question, a matter apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, at that particular time, we're talking about the period after Tito's death, are you disputing that what was expressed most at that time was Albanian extremism and nationalism? Would you challenge that at all?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The official policy or, rather, the policies of the security service was that, yes, Albanian nationalism and extremism was being expressed most. Now, whether that was correct objectively speaking was another matter. But that was the official position taken by the security Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. service and administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, is that right or not? Was that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: For a time, perhaps it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Now, you go on to say that the military leadership, and you say that on page 3, paragraph 4, but I'm sure you'll recall what you said in your statement, that the security administration proposed that -- and suggested that Kosovo military conscripts were sent to do their service as far away from Kosovo as possible, to serve their military obligations because there were armed Albanians in the area. Now, tell me please, General --

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I did my military service, I did it in Zadar, the coastal town of Zadar. Is it not true that it was standard practice in the SFRY for recruits, conscripts from, for example, one republic should do their military service in quite another republic and not do their military service in their own republic, region or town? For example, in the 1960s I did my military service. I'm from Pozarevac and I went to do my military service in Zadar. So that was standard practice. Recruits would be sent throughout Yugoslavia because that too expressed a sort of Yugoslav character that the army had. It was one of the components making up the Yugoslav character of the army. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So many Croats, for example, did their military services in Serbia, Macedonia, Slovenia, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as for your assertion that I said a moment ago and you confirmed it and I quoted it regarding Kosovo, was an additional reason for that precisely the fact that Albanian separatism was burgeoning and that it had flared up and that there was brutal demonstration of that particular nationalism and separatism? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be the subject of a deep discussion, a more profound discussion. In certain units, by the by, of the JNA, regardless of the number of soldiers, Albanian soldiers, which exist -- and there are always most of them in the ground forces for understandable reasons, reasons that were common knowledge, there was a great deal of Albanian nationalism, under inverted commas and irredentism as we used to call it at the time, that was the term we used and others having the same number of soldiers, this was not rampant. Now, what does this indicate? It shows that certain officers, security officers, and first and foremost this took place in the latter half of the 1980s in the areas of the Sarajevo army, that's what it was called then the Sarajevo army, then on the territory of the Belgrade army, that what was covered was large numbers of what we referred to as illegal groups. Now, these same Albanians, Albanians of that kind in other units, where this was not the politics pursued, that is to say to use force to uncover Albanian nationalism, this did not prove to be the case, which indicates again that the treatment of Albanians, the attitude towards Albanians regardless of whether, objectively speaking, they were organising themselves nationalistically or irredentistically that the treatment was adjusted to the political mood of the moment and that enemies were looked for, sought for in the Albanian section of the population. And that's how we felt in other parts of Yugoslavia. And it is my assessment that that proved to be correct ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, General, do you know about the case of soldier Kelmendi? You did refer to it.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was said that he had committed a murder. Later reports showed that perhaps that's not really the way it was, that perhaps it had been rigged. I don't know about that quite fully because I was not in a position to investigate. However, the Kelmendi case was used in all of the JNA for a -- a witch hunt against Albanians. This was just an individual case of a single soldier and it happens anywhere, in any army, in any organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But this soldier killed a number of his fellow soldiers as they were sleeping. There wasn't even a quarrel or a fight before that. There wasn't even an incident of any kind. Quite simply, he used his weapon to kill people around him. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but my answer to that is that there are dozens of incidents taking place nowadays in the US army that an individual commits because he goes crazy, so to speak, under quotation marks. So why are we saying that this was done for nationalistic purposes on Kelmendi's part? This was used in order to create a psychosis of danger. That was my impression of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your opinion, the military leadership and the security administration where you worked, do you feel they did not have reason to be concerned about this particular phenomenon, especially after that case that we just referred to? I'm talking about Albanian nationalism?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I think there was no reason for that and I think individuals from the security administration, and from the security services in general in the JNA, took advantage of that situation for going on this hunt against Albanian soldiers and for no reason whatsoever. For example, in the 5th Air Force Corps where I was head of security, there was not a single Albanian group that was illegally organised. And we never had less than 7 or 800 Albanian soldiers, as opposed to some others like Sarajevo, the Sarajevo district where Mr. Vasiljevic was. Then also some units in the territory of Serbia where there were other chiefs of security who kept finding illegal troikas of Albanians all the time. And it was sufficient for them to get three Albanian names and to claim that this was a group. I was in this environment, and I know that that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was this year when you were in this environment?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Kosovo. I'm talking about the army, the army. This was 1986, 1987, 1988 when people would come from the security administration, specifically Colonel Bogdan Vujic as a specialist, under quotation marks, for the Albanian irredenta. And he would ask for a list of Albanian soldiers in the unit concerned. And then according to that list, he would make up lists of troikas, of illegal groups. I was there and I opposed those methods. From then onwards, I was not really well liked among the security administration people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
