utterances.text: All right. But if you say this was 1986 and in 1991 you were chief of security of the 5th Corps, one really couldn't put it that way that because of this position of yours you suffered certain consequences.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This was one of the details where I disagreed with my superiors, superior officers. Other details of my military career were different and indicated different things. So perhaps that is the reason for my success.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that actually these things were on the rise immediately after Tito's death, after 1980? In 1981 already there were demonstrations by Albanians in Kosovo. Kosovo Republika was the slogan and so on and so together. And then what we're discussing now was probably and after effect of the things that happened then and this did not start only immediately after Tito's death. You remember the demonstrations in 1965 and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So one cannot really say that these are disturbed individuals, a deranged individual. Of course, whoever kills his comrades while they are sleeping is a deranged individual, but here there was a justifiable concern on the part of the security administration. Is that right or is that not right, General?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The assessment was that this was done for nationalist reasons, and this was the assessment that prevailed in JNA structures and also throughout Yugoslav society. Now, whether it was objectively that way or not is now a question that was really up to the people who investigated the matter. For a long time now, I've seen matters differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say in the structures that the entire Yugoslav society, do you remember how many prominent Slovenians, Croats, Muslims, Macedonians and others wrote about that at the time? So it was not the product of Serb nationalism of any kind. It was something that was written about throughout Yugoslav society. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. A lot was written about it, and this was a subject of interest throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, tell me, why are you saying that the one of the major successes of General Vasiljevic was the trial of Officers Ademi and Rrahim and that this was some kind of a fabrication - how should I put this? - something that was artificially created and that nobody knows what the reasons were for bringing charges against these persons? Let me just assist you with the best of intentions. Your former colleague, in all fairness, he held a lower rank than you did, Mustafa Candic, he testified here and he gave rather precise information about this case and why these persons had charged brought against them.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: From 1991 onwards, I talked a great deal to Albanians who were either charged with Albanian nationalism and irredentism or suspected of such things. And the case of Rrahim Ademi convinced me over 100 per cent, if that is at all possible, that he was not encumbered by any kind of nationalism. He did not do anything illegal. He did not organise soldiers, and this was part of the indictment raised against him. I can give you again the example of the 5th Corps where there were officers and junior officers and soldiers, hundreds. There was no Albanian nationalism and irredentism there. And it proved true now in what happened in 1989 in Kosovo, that the officers and the NCOs from the 5th Corps did not take part in everything that happened on the irredenta side, if that's what we can call it now-a-days. So they were not illegally organised. It is quite simply the truth. So General Vasiljevic was really working hard on this and the mentioned Bogdan Vujovic too and the others individuals from the security administration. They were playing this up. And there was a different purpose for all of this. Later on, that also proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what could have been the motive? For example, my impression was although General Vasiljevic here testified here against me, sitting in that very same chair, my impression was that General Vasiljevic was a general with a Yugoslav orientation. Is that your assessment that he was a Yugoslav-oriented General or was he some kind of a Serb nationalist?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I have a high regard for General Vasiljevic as a professional, as a person at the time when I knew him. However, in 1991, he placed himself in the service of war against the Republic of Croatia; that is to say in the interests of one of the Yugoslav peoples. So from that point of view I do not have a high regard for him. But in terms of professionalism, until then I can only congratulate him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, he's the one who discovered the illegal import of weapons. Wasn't that his duty? He was head of security. Wasn't this the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. against the interests of Yugoslavia and wasn't this the task of the security service, to stop this, to discover this, and to render it impossible?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This was his task, but then on the other hand, it's also debatable whether this should have been his task or whether it should have been the task of the state security. So there's a major dilemma in this respect. That is one point. Because according to the rules of service, the JNA security organs could not work outside JNA structures and that's exactly what he was doing. Secondly, once he discovered this, once he saw that he saw that one of the republics was arming itself, in this case the Republic of Croatia, he should have studied this in depth. He should have seen why this was being done and he should have insisted with the military leadership and asked them to take a different position with regard to resolving the JNA crisis. And I think that the JNA leadership, had they taken a different view, there would have been a peaceful break-up of Yugoslavia and there wouldn't have been this many victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's now quarter to. It's time to adjourn, I think. I see Mr. Nice is here. I don't know if he has fresh dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, you have two hours on Monday morning with this witness, which will give you the same as the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday we got an information from the witness unit that General Agotic needs to be in Croatia on Monday. I wonder whether this could be solved and whether he is available on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, what -- can you tell us your position on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could finish today if at all possible, but I certainly don't want to upset your schedule in any way, but I do have some engagements in Zagreb on Monday that I had planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'd be grateful if you would be here on Monday, because it's not possible for us to sit this afternoon. There's another case coming in. Could you try and reschedule your engagements? We'll try and make sure you're away as quickly as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is necessary, I would kindly ask that I be the first on Monday morning so that I could catch a plane to Zagreb and be there in the evening if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That we can assure you of. Yes. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
